   No Constant-Cost Protocol for Point–Line Incidence
        Mika Göös      Nathaniel Harms             Florian K. Richter             Anastasia Sofronova
           EPFL                  UBC                          EPFL                              EPFL

                                                April 7, 2026


                                                    Abstract
      Alice and Bob are given n-bit integer pairs (x, y) and (a, b), respectively, and they must decide
      if y = ax + b. We prove that the randomised communication complexity of this Point–Line
      Incidence problem is Θ(log n). This confirms a conjecture of Cheung, Hatami, Hosseini, and
      Shirley (CCC 2023) that the complexity is super-constant, and gives the first example of a
      communication problem with constant support-rank but super-constant randomised complexity.

1    Introduction
Given n-bit integers x, y, a, b, how hard is it to check whether
                                            y = ax + b?

In communication complexity, we suppose Alice has (x, y) and Bob has (a, b). How many bits
of communication are required for them to check this equation? This is the simplest arithmetic
(in)equality whose randomised communication complexity is not yet known. For comparison, the
randomised complexities of y = ax, y ⩾ b, and y ⩾ ax + b are fully understood; see Table 1.
    The problem of deciding y = ax + b is known as Point–Line Incidence (PL). To our
annoyance, it is a priori unclear if this can be solved by even a constant-cost randomised protocol,
that is, with cost independent of n. Indeed, there is no known structural criterion that rules out
a constant-cost protocol for PL, despite it being such a natural problem (see Section 1.3 for the
ongoing quest to find such structural criteria). Cheung, Hatami, Hosseini, and Shirley [CHHS23]
conjectured that it does not have a constant-cost protocol. We confirm their conjecture:

Theorem 1. The public-coin randomised communication complexity of PL is Ω(log n).

    This is tight: there is an O(log n)-bit randomised protocol as observed by [CLV19]. The players
choose a random prime p ⩽ O(n), Alice sends x and y modulo p, and Bob checks whether y = ax+b
(mod p). This protocol has one-sided error, because if y = ax + b then this remains true modulo p.
    The same idea gives a protocol for the more general problem of checking ki=1 xi yi = 0 for n-bit
                                                                             P
integers xi , yi . This is Integer Inner Product [CLV19, CHHS23, CHH+ 25]. As a corollary, we
get tight bounds on this problem as well, stated in Section 1.2. These results witness the first
separation between randomised communication and support-rank, which we discuss in Section 1.1.

1.1   Consequences for Rank Measures
Since y = ax + b is a simple polynomial equation, it has low algebraic complexity as formalised by
support- and sign-rank. These are defined for a two-party function f : X × Y → {0, 1} as follows.
 • Support-rank rank0 (f ) is the smallest dimension r ∈ N in which f can be represented by linear
   equalities; that is, such that there exist embeddings ϕ : X → Rr and ψ : Y → Rr with

                            ∀x, y :        f (x, y) = 0   ⇐⇒    ⟨ϕ(x), ψ(y)⟩ = 0.

   In other words, the support-rank of f , viewed as a |X |-by-|Y| boolean matrix, is the least rank
   of a matrix M ∈ RX ×Y that has the same support as f . Previously, support-rank has been
   called nondeterministic rank in quantum communication complexity [dW03], equality rank in
   circuit complexity [HP10], and minimum rank in graph theory [FH07].

 • Sign-rank rank± (f ) is the smallest dimension r ∈ N in which f can be represented by linear
   inequalities; that is, such that there exist embeddings ϕ : X → Rr and ψ : Y → Rr with

                                 ∀x, y :       ⟨ϕ(x), ψ(y)⟩ · (−1)f (x,y) > 0.

   Sign-rank is known to be equivalent to unbounded-error randomised communication, where the
   two parties have private randomness and must succeed with probability > 1/2 [PS86]. Sign-rank
   is much more powerful than support-rank: Every problem of support-rank r has sign-rank O(r2 )
   (see, e.g., [GHIS25]), while there are problems over n := log max(|X |, |Y|) input bits with sign-
   rank 2 and support-rank 2n (e.g., Greater-Than).
For Point–Line Incidence, the embeddings ϕ(x, y) = (x, y, 1) and ψ(a, b) = (a, −1, b) show
that the support-rank of the negation ¬PL is at most 3. Consequently, Theorem 1 implies the
following separation of support-rank and public-coin randomised communication complexity R(f );
previously, it was not known whether rank0 (f ) = O(1) implies R(f ) = O(1).
Corollary 2. There is an f with rank0 (f ) ⩽ 3 and R(f ) ⩾ ω(1).

                                                      2
   The analogous separation for sign-rank has been long known: Greater-Than has sign-rank 2
but randomised complexity Ω(log n) [BW15, Vio15, SY23]. For support-rank, the separation in
Corollary 2 is qualitatively the best possible, in the sense that all problems of support-rank 2
reduce to Equality and therefore have randomised complexity O(1). On the other hand, proving
a more dramatic quantitative separation for an n-bit problem remains open:
Open Problem 3. Is there an f with rank0 (f ) ⩽ O(1) and R(f ) ⩾ nΩ(1) ?
   The analogous separation for sign-rank was recently obtained by [HHL20, ACHS24]. They
exhibit problems with sign-rank 3 that have randomised complexity Θ(n). In fact, this holds for
the Halfplane Membership problem of deciding whether y ⩾ ax + b.

1.2   Integer Inner Product, and Motivation from Oracle Protocols
In the Integer Inner Product (IIPkn ) problem Alice andPBob receive n-bit integers x1 , . . . , xk
and y1 , . . . , yk , respectively, and they want to check whether ki=1 xi yi = 0. As already mentioned,
this problem has randomised complexity O(k log n) [CLV19]. We get a matching lower bound:
Corollary 4. The public-coin randomised communication complexity of IIPkn is Ω(k log n) for
every 3 ⩽ k ⩽ nε where ε > 0 is some constant.
     The condition k ⩽ nε is most likely an artefact of our technique. Nevertheless, it is only a mild
restriction since for large k there is also an Ω(k) lower bound by a reduction from Disjointness.
     Integer Inner Product was introduced by [CLV19] to show that efficient randomised pro-
tocols cannot be simulated by the Equality oracle. Specifically, they showed that IIP6n has no
efficient protocol if we are only allowed to use randomness to solve instances of Equality. In
their words, “Equality alone does not simulate randomness.” In fact, Equality doesn’t help in
this problem at all: a deterministic protocol with access to an Equality oracle still requires Ω(n)
bits of communication. We write this result as DEq (IIP6n ) ⩾ Ω(n), where DEq (f ) is the number
of Equality queries required to compute f . This was improved to hold for PL by [CHHS23]
and simplified by [CHH+ 25]. It remains open whether it is possible to push this type of separation
further: the papers [CHHS23, GHR25] ask whether a similar lower bound against Equality-oracle
protocols holds for some problem with constant randomised complexity:
Open Problem 5. Is there a problem f with R(f ) ⩽ O(1) but DEq (f ) ⩾ Ω(n)?
   This was the initial context for the conjecture R(PL) ⩾ ω(1) of [CHHS23], because if Point–
Line Incidence had a constant-cost protocol, it would have resolved this question. In light of our
Theorem 1, the question remains open. Currently, the best lower bound against Equality-oracle
                                                          √
protocols for a problem with R(f ) ⩽ O(1) is DEq (f ) ⩾ Ω( n) [GHR25].

1.3   Motivation from Constant-Cost Communication
Our results fit more broadly within a recent line of work on “constant-cost” communication. Tra-
ditionally, communication complexity tries to classify n-bit communication problems into easy
problems that can be solved with (log n)O(1) bits of communication and hard problems that re-
quire nΩ(1) bits. The papers [HHH23, HWZ22] proposed to consider the constant-cost complexity
dichotomy O(1)-vs-ω(1) instead of the traditional (log n)O(1) -vs-nΩ(1) . This provides a new “sand-
box” where we can study old questions from a novel perspective, helping us develop new lower-bound
methods, and also to discover new questions interesting in their own right.

                                                   3
Class BPP0 . A central mystery in this new theory asks to characterise all total problems f
that have constant randomised complexity, R(f ) ⩽ O(1). This class of problems, denoted BPP0 ,
captures the most extreme ways in which randomness can benefit protocols. It has been heavily in-
vestigated in recent work [HHH22, EHK22, HHP+ 22, HZ24, FHHH24, FGHH25, GHR25, BHT25].
The class has many equivalent definitions (constant discrepancy, point–halfspace arrangements with
constant margin, PAC learnable under pure differential privacy [FX14]), but all of them so far are
“semantic,” hiding a promise. Since constant-cost protocols seem very restrictive, one may hope
for a simple “syntactic” characterisation. Various natural candidates for a characterisation have
been disproved: the class admits no complete problem [FHHH24]; nor certain complete hierar-
chies [FGHH25, GHR25]. Theorem 1 poses a challenge for any such characterisation, which must
somehow generalise our highly-tailored lower bound argument (at least qualitatively).

Class UPP0 . The second-most prominent constant-cost class is UPP0 that contains all total prob-
lems with a constant-cost unbounded-error protocol, that is, problems of constant sign-rank [PS86].
As discussed above, Greater-Than shows that UPP0 ̸⊆ BPP0 and our Corollary 2 upgrades this
to a separation SUPP0 ̸⊆ BPP0 where SUPP0 ⊆ UPP0 is the class of problems with constant
support-rank, defined in [GHIS25]. The converse separation has grown into a nagging problem:

Open Problem 6. Show that BPP0 ̸⊆ UPP0 .

   This separation has been shown for partial functions by Hatami, Hosseini, and Meng [HHM23].
Towards a separation for total functions, one might first ask to show the weaker separation BPP0 ̸⊆
SUPP0 . But this already follows by considering the Equality problem, which has support-rank 2n
on n-bit inputs. A better first step is the following, asked in [GHIS25].

Open Problem 7. Show that BPP0 ̸⊆ PSUPP
                                   0    .

   Here PSUPP
           0      is the class of problems expressible as boolean combinations of constantly many
problems of constant support-rank. This dispenses with Equality as a separating example since its
complement has constant support-rank. It is known that PSUPP0    ⊆ UPP0 [GHIS25] so this is truly a
necessary first step towards Open Problem 6. For more discussion on constant-cost communication
complexity, we recommend the excellent survey of Hatami and Hatami [HH24].
